extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning introductory combinatorics / proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and standards for counting finite lists, permutations, k-permutations, and subsets: using multiplication, addition, and subtraction (complement) principles; factorials; P(n,k) and binomial coefficients; and practical casework strategies to avoid double-counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: When building a list (or performing a sequence of choices) where each step has a fixed number of independent choices, the total number of outcomes is the product of the number of choices at each step (e.g., 7·6·5·4 = 840 for non-repetitive length-4 lists from 7 symbols).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when choices for each position are independent or when you've accounted for dependence by adjusting the counts for each step (examples: counting non-repetitive lists by reducing available choices each time). Use as the basic tool for counting sequences, codes, strings, and ordered outcomes. Anti-pattern: do not multiply raw per-slot maxima when later slots' available choices depend on earlier selections unless you explicitly incorporate that dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double-counting (overlap caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: When breaking a counting problem into types/cases, ensure that the types are pairwise disjoint; otherwise some outcomes will be counted multiple times (example: counting lists with at least one E by summing counts of lists with E in each position double/triple-counts lists where E occurs multiple times).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If types overlap, either refine them to be disjoint (e.g., specify exact multiplicity/location patterns) or use a different method (like subtraction/complement or inclusion–exclusion when appropriate). The textbook example shows naive summation gave 1372 whereas correct complement method gave 1105.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition Principle (disjoint union)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact 3.2: Suppose a finite set X can be decomposed as a union X = X1 ∪ X2 ∪ ... ∪ Xn, where Xi ∩ Xj = ∅ whenever i ≠ j. Then |X| = |X1| + |X2| + ... + |Xn|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when you can partition the target set into disjoint, easier-to-count pieces (example: lists containing exactly one E partitioned by the position of the E). Important requirement: intersections must be empty; otherwise you'll overcount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtraction Principle (complement counting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact 3.3: If X is a subset of a finite set U, then |U − X| = |U| − |X|. Equivalently, to count elements having a property, sometimes it's easier to count all possibilities and subtract those without the property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when the complement is easier to count than the target set (examples: "lists with at least one E" counted as total lists minus lists with no E; "lists with at least one repeated letter" counted as total lists minus non-repetitive lists). This is the recommended method when naive case-summing leads to overlap issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case decomposition by explicit types (disjoint cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide the set of outcomes into explicit types or categories based on a distinguishing feature (e.g., which position contains a particular symbol) and count each type separately provided these types are disjoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works hand-in-hand with the multiplication and addition principles: count each type with multiplication and sum using the addition principle. Example: length-4 non-repetitive lists containing exactly one E are split into four disjoint types depending on E's position, each counted as 6·5·4 = 120 and summed to 480.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fill restricted positions first
rubrics_metrics.description: When restrictions make the number of options for later positions dependent on earlier choices (so the multiplication principle is awkward), fill the positions that have constraints first (e.g., fill first and last boxes that have restrictions before filling middle boxes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strategy avoids uncertainty about available choices later. Example: for non-repetitive length-5 lists where the first must be B/C/D and the last must be a vowel, fill first and last first, then count permutations of remaining symbols for the middle positions to get 3·5·4·3·2 = 360.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorial definition and properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 3.1: If n is a non-negative integer, then n! is the number of lists of length n that can be made from n symbols, without repetition. Thus 0! = 1, 1! = 1, and for n > 1, n! = n(n−1)(n−2)·...·3·2·1. Also n! = n·(n−1)!.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use factorials to count permutations of an entire n-element set. Remember the base case 0! = 1 (important for algebraic identities and combinatorial formulas). Factorials are used to compactly express permutation and combination formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permutation of a set (full permutation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A permutation of a set is an arrangement of all of the set's elements in a row (a list without repetition using every element). An n-element set has n! permutations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret reorderings of all elements (e.g., seating arrangements, full orderings) as permutations; use n! for counting. Example: 20 students seated in numbered desks gives 20! permutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: k-permutation and P(n,k)
rubrics_metrics.description: A k-permutation of an n-element set is a non-repetitive list of length k made from elements of the set. P(n,k) = n(n−1)(n−2)·...·(n−k+1). For 0 < k ≤ n, P(n,k) = n!/(n−k)!; P(n,0) = 1; P(n,k) = 0 when k > n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use P(n,k) to count ordered selections of k distinct elements from n (e.g., podium places, ordered draws). Use the factorial quotient form for computation convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial coefficient (n choose k) and counting k-element subsets
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition: (n choose k) denotes the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set. Fact 3.5: For 0 ≤ k ≤ n, (n choose k) = n! / (k!(n−k)!). If k < 0 or k > n then (n choose k) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count unordered selections (hands, combinations) with (n choose k). Derivation: count all k-permutations and divide by k! (the number of orderings of each chosen subset). Examples: number of 5-card poker hands is (52 choose 5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiply choices across independent categories (product of combinations)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a selection consists of independent choices from disjoint categories (e.g., choose 2 clubs and 3 hearts), count choices in each category and multiply (e.g., (13 choose 2)·(13 choose 3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each categorical choice as an independent subproblem counted by combinations or permutations, then apply the multiplication principle. Example: counting 5-card hands with exactly 2 clubs and 3 hearts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use addition principle for counting by counts of a property (e.g., number of 1's)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the property of interest partitions outcomes by a count (e.g., strings with 1, 3, 5, or 7 ones), compute sizes of each partition and sum them. Example: number of 7-bit strings with an odd number of 1's equals (7 choose 1)+(7 choose 3)+(7 choose 5)+(7 choose 7)=64.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break by exact count of the feature and ensure partitions are disjoint (distinct counts are disjoint). This is a standard application of the addition principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complement strategy for 'at least one' and 'at most' problems
rubrics_metrics.description: For "at least one" problems, count total possibilities and subtract those with none of the property (complement). Similarly, for 'at least one repeated letter' count total lists minus those with no repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a special case of the subtraction principle and helps avoid messy inclusion of overlapping cases. Example calculations: 7^4 total lists minus 6^4 with no E gives 1105 lists containing at least one E.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitfall: naive per-slot multiplication when availability varies
rubrics_metrics.description: If the number of choices for a later slot depends on what was chosen earlier (e.g., vowels might be used up), naive multiplication using the same count for each slot will be incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect dependencies and either (a) count conditional on earlier choices and multiply accordingly, (b) fill constrained slots first, or (c) use complementary or partitioning methods to avoid uncertain per-slot counts.
